pivot: Whether SB 53's frontier-developer obligations (framework disclosure, critical-safety-incident reporting to Cal OES) are pled, filed on, or ruled to reach the undisclosed internal-deployment conduct within ~90 days of attribution
pivot_observable: A CA AG filing, Cal OES incident-report record, or court/agency ruling that names internal-deployment conduct as within SB 53's covered scope — versus the absence of any such filing by the date below
pivot_because: If this resolves YES, ai-regulation-teeth's clean operator/developer split breaks (a developer faces consequence under a pre-incident statute), ai-oversight-lag's anchoring claim breaks (trigger no longer confined to deployment status), and ai-pressure/lab-moves/ai-public-backlash's shared 'gap stays open' picture flips for all three at once, because they inherit the same unargued premise. If it resolves NO, the five-minute consensus stands intact. No rival variable does this: the federal-endorsement question (ai-pressure) is a signal about posture, not an instrument operating inside the 90-day window; the ~Dec-15 deployer-liability instrument (ai-public-backlash) lands the same either way; lab-moves' compliance-posture claim is downstream of, not independent from, this pivot.
rival_pivots_rejected: ai-pressure's federal-preemption-vehicle question (does the executive flip to endorsing Thune/Cruz/Klobuchar) is not the hinge: even if it resolves either way, the five-minute bloc's 'gap stays open' claim and pressure-model's 'gap gets tested' claim are unaffected — the federal bill is a parallel track, not a determinant of whether SB 53 itself gets tested. ai-public-backlash's 'does a pre-drafted deployer instrument clear by ~12-15' is not the hinge either: it is compatible with both branches of the real pivot and several minutes treat it as background motion rather than the deciding fact. lab-moves' 'does the implicated developer take a public compliance posture' is a consequence of market/reputation pressure that plays out regardless of how the SB 53 reach question resolves, so it reorders confidence, not the outcome set.
ruling: The case turns on whether SB 53's frontier-developer obligations get tested against the undisclosed-internal-deployment conduct within the 90-day window: if a filing or ruling reaches it, the five-minute consensus (gap stays open, correction hardens only at the release/operator gate) breaks across all five at once; if none does, that consensus holds and the incident's correction pressure stays confined to deployment-gated, operator-facing instruments.
because: Five of six minutes rely on the same unargued premise — that existing and pre-drafted instruments scope to deployment status and identifiable operator, so undisclosed internal deployment stays outside reach — without any of them arguing why SB 53's text excludes it; they inherit rather than defend this. pressure-model is the only minute to attack that premise directly, and it is the only round-2 REVISE, sharpening from a vague 'duty of care' reference to SB 53's actual named obligations (framework disclosure, Cal OES incident reporting), which makes its claim the one that is both reorder-capable and checkable on a specific near-term clock.
threat_live: Attributable-incident correction hardens at the release/operator gate and, in doing so, legitimizes the internal-deployment gap as outside scope — the regime looks responsive while AI-on-AI chains triggered by undisclosed internal deployment remain uncovered (ai-oversight-lag, lab-moves). Newly dangerous on the other branch: if the federal duty-of-care vehicle with express preemption advances (ai-pressure), it could foreclose the state-level test case pressure-model's pivot depends on, before SB 53 is ever tested against this conduct.
strongest_minute: pressure-model — it is the only minute that names a variable capable of reordering the other five's outcomes rather than just shading confidence within their shared frame, and it is the only minute that revised its own claim in round 2 to sharpen the mechanism into something dated and checkable.
weakest_minute: ai-pressure — its 'because' cites its own internal premise (P6, installer-credibility branching) rather than arguing the claim, and its federal-flip claim smuggles a second assumption (a specific named bill, a current unilateral-preemption posture) the brief never granted.
shared_assumption: That SB 53 (or any pre-incident instrument) scopes by deployment status and identifiable operator, and therefore does not reach undisclosed internal deployment — asserted by five minutes as a starting condition rather than argued from the statute's text.
smuggled_assumption: ai-pressure assumes a specific federal vehicle (the Thune/Cruz/Klobuchar bill) and a prior unilateral-preemption executive posture as background facts; the brief grants only the incident and its attribution, not the current state of federal legislative alignment.
unresolved: Whether the incident's own causal chain runs through the undisclosed internal deployment (which would make the SB 53 reach question directly justiciable on these facts) or through an external/deployed surface only (which would make pressure-model's test case hypothetical) — the minutes assert both framings (oversight-lag's 'chained AI-on-AI action,' lab-moves' 'deployed-system incident') without reconciling them.
